lessons.title: Macro minerals: calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, potassium
lessons.body: Macro minerals are needed in large amounts, measured in grams per day. For a 400 kg steer gaining 1 kg per day, you need about 30 g calcium (Ca) and 20 g phosphorus (P). The ideal Ca:P ratio is between 1.5:1 and 2:1. If you feed too much phosphorus and too little calcium, the steer can get urinary stones, especially in males. In Africa, many forages are low in phosphorus, particularly in the dry season. A simple test: if cattle chew bones or eat soil, they likely need phosphorus. Common sources: limestone (38% Ca), bone meal (30% Ca, 15% P), and dicalcium phosphate (23% Ca, 18% P). For magnesium, a 400 kg steer needs about 10 g per day. Grass tetany (hypomagnesemia) occurs when grazing lush, cool-season grasses low in magnesium. Prevent it by feeding 30 g of magnesium oxide per head per day during risky periods. Potassium is usually abundant in forages, but young, rapidly growing grasses can be low. A steer needs about 25 g potassium daily. Deficiency causes poor appetite and weight loss. In Africa, potassium deficiency is rare except on very sandy soils or during drought. Always provide a mineral mix with the correct ratios. A simple on-farm mix: 50 kg limestone, 30 kg dicalcium phosphate, 10 kg salt, 5 kg magnesium oxide, and 5 kg trace mineral premix. This provides roughly 40% Ca, 10% P, and 5% Mg. Mix well and offer free choice. Monitor intake: cattle should eat 50â100 g per head per day. If they eat more, add salt; if less, add molasses powder.

lessons.title: Micro minerals: zinc, copper, manganese, selenium
lessons.body: Micro minerals are needed in tiny amountsâmilligrams or micrograms per dayâbut they are critical. For a 400 kg steer, you need about 30 mg zinc (Zn), 10 mg copper (Cu), 20 mg manganese (Mn), and 0.1 mg selenium (Se) per kg of dry matter intake. In Africa, copper deficiency is common in cattle grazing on sandy or high-molybdenum soils. Signs include dull coat, diarrhea, and poor growth. A simple fix: give a copper bolus twice a year or add copper sulfate to the mineral mix at 0.5% (5 g per kg of mix). But be careful: sheep are very sensitive to copper, so never feed cattle minerals to sheep. Zinc deficiency causes rough skin, slow wound healing, and reduced fertility. Add zinc sulfate at 0.5% of the mineral mix. Manganese is needed for bone development and reproduction. Deficiency is rare but can occur on heavily leached soils. Use manganese sulfate at 0.3% of the mix. Selenium is the most critical: deficiency causes white muscle disease in calves and poor fertility in cows. In many parts of Africa, soils are selenium-deficient. You can give a selenium injection (e.g., 1 ml per 50 kg body weight of a 0.5% selenium solution) every 3â4 months, or add sodium selenite to the mineral mix at 0.01% (100 mg per kg of mix). Never exceed 0.3 mg selenium per kg of total dietâit is toxic. A good trace mineral premix for cattle in Africa should contain per kg: 20 g Zn, 10 g Cu, 15 g Mn, 0.2 g Se, 0.5 g I, and 0.1 g Co. Mix 5 kg of this premix into 100 kg of macro mineral mix. Always store minerals in a dry place; moisture destroys potency.

lessons.title: Vitamin requirements: A, D, E, and K
lessons.body: Vitamins are needed in small amounts but are essential for health and growth. For a 400 kg steer, you need about 2,200 IU of vitamin A per kg of dry matter, 275 IU of vitamin D, and 15 IU of vitamin E. Vitamin K is usually synthesized by rumen microbes, so deficiency is rare unless the animal eats moldy sweet clover. In Africa, vitamin A deficiency is common in dry-season grazing because green forage is scarce. Signs include night blindness, rough coat, and poor growth. You can inject vitamin A (e.g., 1 million IU per animal) every 2â3 months, or add a stabilized vitamin A premix to the mineral mix at 500,000 IU per kg of mix. Vitamin D is made in the skin from sunlight, so deficiency is rare in sunny Africa. However, cattle kept indoors or in very cloudy regions may need supplementation. Add 100,000 IU per kg of mineral mix. Vitamin E works with selenium; deficiency causes white muscle disease. Add 500 IU per kg of mineral mix. For a simple home mix: 1 kg of vitamin premix (containing 500,000 IU vitamin A, 100,000 IU vitamin D, and 500 IU vitamin E per gram) mixed into 100 kg of mineral mix. This provides enough vitamins for 100 cattle for one day if they eat 50 g each. Always check expiry datesâvitamins lose potency over time. Store in a cool, dark place. If you cannot find a premix, you can use cod liver oil (rich in A and D) at 10 ml per animal per week, but it is messy and less precise.

lessons.title: Bioavailability of mineral sources
lessons.body: Bioavailability means how much of a mineral the animal can actually absorb and use. Not all sources are equal. For calcium, limestone is cheap but only 30â40% available. Dicalcium phosphate is 90% available for both calcium and phosphorus. For phosphorus, bone meal is 80â90% available, but rock phosphate is only 50â60% available and may contain fluoride, which is toxic. In Africa, many farmers use bone meal from local abattoirsâit is a good source if properly sterilized. For zinc, zinc sulfate is 40â50% available, while zinc oxide is only 20â30% available. So if you use zinc oxide, you need to double the amount. For copper, copper sulfate is 50â60% available, but copper oxide is only 10â20% available. Always use copper sulfate in mineral mixes. For selenium, sodium selenite is 70â80% available, while selenium yeast is 90â95% available but more expensive. For magnesium, magnesium oxide is 50â60% available, but magnesium sulfate is 80â90% availableâhowever, it is laxative. In practice, use magnesium oxide in mineral mixes. For vitamins, natural sources (green forage) are highly available, but synthetic vitamins in premixes are stable and predictable. When formulating, always use the available amount, not the total amount. For example, if you need 20 g phosphorus and you use bone meal (15% P, 80% available), you need 20 / (0.15 * 0.8) = 167 g bone meal per animal per day. This is why accurate formulation matters. Test your mineral sources if possibleâsimple kits are available from agricultural suppliers.

lessons.title: Mineral interactions and antagonists
lessons.body: Minerals do not work alone. They interact, and some block the absorption of others. The most famous is the copper-molybdenum-sulfur interaction. If your forage has more than 2 ppm molybdenum and 0.2% sulfur, copper absorption drops sharply. In Africa, this is common in pastures near mining areas or on high-molybdenum soils. To fix it, increase copper in the mineral mix by 50% or more. Another interaction: high calcium blocks zinc absorption. If your Ca:P ratio is above 4:1, zinc deficiency can occur even if you supplement zinc. Keep the ratio between 1.5:1 and 2:1. High phosphorus blocks magnesium absorption, so avoid excess phosphorus when preventing grass tetany. High iron blocks copper and zinc. If your water has high iron (common in boreholes), you may need extra copper and zinc. High sulfur (from water or feed) blocks selenium and copper. In Africa, many boreholes have high sulfur. Test your water. Also, excess potassium blocks magnesium. If you feed lush young grass high in potassium, add extra magnesium. Antagonists can be managed by: 1) Testing your forage and water for mineral content; 2) Adjusting the mineral mix to account for antagonists; 3) Using chelated minerals (bound to amino acids) which are less affected by antagonists, but they are expensive. A practical rule: if you see deficiency signs despite supplementing, consider an antagonist. For example, if cattle show copper deficiency signs but you are feeding copper, test for molybdenum and sulfur. Simple on-farm fix: add 1% copper sulfate and 0.5% zinc sulfate to your mineral mix if you suspect high antagonists.

lessons.title: Formulating mineral supplements and premixes
lessons.body: Formulating a mineral supplement is like following a recipe. You need to know the requirements of your cattle, the mineral content of your feeds, and the bioavailability of your sources. Start with a base mix of macro minerals. For a 400 kg steer, a good daily mix might be: 50 g limestone (for calcium), 30 g dicalcium phosphate (for phosphorus), 10 g salt, 5 g magnesium oxide, and 5 g trace mineral premix. This gives about 20 g calcium, 5 g phosphorus, and 3 g magnesium. But you must adjust based on your forage. If your grass is low in phosphorus (common in Africa), increase dicalcium phosphate to 50 g. If you are in a grass tetany area, increase magnesium oxide to 10 g. For trace minerals, use a commercial premix if available. If not, make your own: mix 20 kg zinc sulfate, 10 kg copper sulfate, 15 kg manganese sulfate, 0.2 kg sodium selenite, 0.5 kg potassium iodide, and 0.1 kg cobalt sulfate with 54 kg of ground maize or limestone as a carrier. This makes 100 kg of trace mineral premix. Add 5 kg of this premix to 100 kg of macro mix. For vitamins, add 1 kg of vitamin premix (containing A, D, E) to 100 kg of mineral mix. Mix thoroughly on a clean concrete floor or in a drum mixer. Store in airtight bags in a dry place. Offer free choice in covered mineral feeders. Cattle should eat 50â100 g per head per day. If they eat too much, add 10% salt; if too little, add 5% molasses powder. Monitor body condition and health. Adjust every 3 months based on season and forage quality. Always keep records of your formulations and intakes.

quiz.q: What is the ideal calcium to phosphorus ratio for cattle?
quiz.explanation: The ideal Ca:P ratio is between 1.5:1 and 2:1 to prevent urinary stones and ensure proper bone development.

quiz.q: Which mineral deficiency causes grass tetany?
quiz.explanation: Grass tetany is caused by low magnesium in the blood, often when grazing lush, cool-season grasses.

quiz.q: How much magnesium oxide should you feed to prevent grass tetany?
options: A) 5 g per head per day
B) 10 g per head per day
C) 30 g per head per day
D) 100 g per head per day
quiz.explanation: Feeding 30 g of magnesium oxide per head per day during risky periods helps prevent grass tetany.

quiz.q: Which macro mineral is usually abundant in forages but can be low in young, rapidly growing grasses?
quiz.explanation: Potassium is usually abundant, but young, rapidly growing grasses can be low, leading to deficiency.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of phosphorus deficiency in cattle?
options: B) Chewing bones or eating soil
quiz.explanation: Cattle with phosphorus deficiency often chew bones or eat soil to try to get more phosphorus.

quiz.q: Which micro mineral deficiency causes white muscle disease in calves?
quiz.explanation: Selenium deficiency, often combined with vitamin E deficiency, causes white muscle disease in calves.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe level of selenium in the total diet?
quiz.explanation: Selenium is toxic above 0.3 mg per kg of total diet, so never exceed this level.

quiz.q: Which mineral is especially toxic to sheep, so cattle minerals should not be fed to sheep?
quiz.explanation: Sheep are very sensitive to copper, and cattle minerals often contain too much copper for sheep.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is usually synthesized by rumen microbes, so deficiency is rare?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin K is synthesized by rumen microbes, so deficiency is rare unless the animal eats moldy sweet clover.

quiz.q: How much vitamin A per kg of dry matter does a 400 kg steer need?
quiz.explanation: A 400 kg steer needs about 2,200 IU of vitamin A per kg of dry matter intake.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is made in the skin from sunlight, so deficiency is rare in sunny Africa?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin D is synthesized in the skin from sunlight, so deficiency is rare in sunny regions.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of vitamin A deficiency in cattle?
quiz.explanation: Night blindness is an early sign of vitamin A deficiency in cattle.

quiz.q: Which source of calcium is most available to cattle?
quiz.explanation: Dicalcium phosphate is about 90% available for calcium, while limestone is only 30-40% available.

quiz.q: Which source of zinc is most available?
quiz.explanation: Zinc sulfate is 40-50% available, while zinc oxide is only 20-30% available.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid rock phosphate as a phosphorus source?
options: B) It contains fluoride which is toxic
C) It is low in phosphorus
D) It is not available in Africa
quiz.explanation: Rock phosphate may contain fluoride, which is toxic to cattle, and its phosphorus is only 50-60% available.

quiz.q: If you need 20 g of available phosphorus and use bone meal (15% P, 80% available), how much bone meal do you need?
quiz.explanation: 20 g / (0.15 * 0.8) = 167 g of bone meal to provide 20 g of available phosphorus.

quiz.q: Which mineral interaction can cause copper deficiency even when copper is supplemented?
quiz.explanation: High molybdenum and sulfur in the diet block copper absorption, leading to deficiency.

quiz.q: What is the maximum Ca:P ratio before zinc absorption is negatively affected?
quiz.explanation: A Ca:P ratio above 4:1 can block zinc absorption, so keep it between 1.5:1 and 2:1.

quiz.q: Which mineral can block magnesium absorption when in excess?
quiz.explanation: High phosphorus blocks magnesium absorption, so avoid excess phosphorus when preventing grass tetany.

quiz.q: What is a practical way to manage mineral antagonists?
options: B) Test forage and water, then adjust the mineral mix
C) Feed more of the same mineral
quiz.explanation: Testing forage and water for mineral content helps you adjust the mineral mix to account for antagonists.

quiz.q: In a mineral mix, what is the purpose of salt?
quiz.explanation: Salt is used to control intake; if cattle eat too much mineral, adding salt reduces consumption.

quiz.q: How much trace mineral premix should be added to 100 kg of macro mineral mix?
quiz.explanation: A typical inclusion rate is 5 kg of trace mineral premix per 100 kg of macro mineral mix.

quiz.q: What should you do if cattle eat too little of the mineral mix?
quiz.explanation: Adding molasses powder improves palatability and increases intake if cattle eat too little.

quiz.q: How often should you adjust your mineral mix based on season and forage quality?
quiz.explanation: Adjusting every 3 months allows you to respond to seasonal changes in forage quality.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is important for blood clotting and is synthesized by rumen microbes?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and is synthesized by rumen microbes, so deficiency is rare.

quiz.q: What is the daily requirement of vitamin E for a 400 kg steer?
options: A) 5 IU per kg dry matter
B) 15 IU per kg dry matter
C) 50 IU per kg dry matter
D) 100 IU per kg dry matter
quiz.explanation: A 400 kg steer needs about 15 IU of vitamin E per kg of dry matter intake.

quiz.q: Which mineral deficiency can cause poor fertility in cows?
quiz.explanation: Zinc, copper, and manganese deficiencies can all lead to poor fertility in cows.

quiz.q: What is a good source of magnesium for mineral mixes?
quiz.explanation: Magnesium oxide is commonly used because it is less laxative than magnesium sulfate and has good availability.

quiz.q: Why is it important to store minerals in a dry place?
quiz.explanation: Moisture can destroy the potency of vitamins and cause minerals to clump, so store in a dry place.

quiz.q: What is the first step in formulating a mineral supplement?
options: B) Know the requirements of your cattle and the mineral content of your feeds
D) Feed it to the cattle
quiz.explanation: You must know the animal's requirements and the mineral content of feeds to formulate an effective supplement.
